newsitem.title: USA: Financial services changes challenge to Fed-Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Financial services changes challenge to Fed-Jordan.

text.p: Technology-driven changes in the financial services industry are a challenge to the future U.S. monetary policy process, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Jerry Jordan said on Tuesday.

"Evolution of the financial services industry carries implications for money and monetary policy," Jordan told a Consumer Bankers Association conference. "The challenge we face at the Fed is to ensure we can adapt our own operating practices and monetary policies to maintain financial stability and control the price level."
Jordan stressed "new payments technologies should be regarded as innovations that enhance productivity and welfare just as surely as any other product."
Such developments were topics discussed at the four-day CBA conference, including "Technology and Personal Financial Services Distribution" and "Stored Value Cards."
The emergence of electronic money, however, is expected to affect one traditional tool of monetary policy -- banks' reserve requirements.
"Today, banks hold our liabilities because they must met reserve requirements," Jordan told the retail bankers.
"They find having Reserve Bank balances instrumental in settling transactions with other banks, and because the public uses Federal Reserve notes in transactions," he added.

"Required reserves are already declining. In the future, the demand for central bank money will depend on the Fed's usefulness in net settlement and on the public's interest in using Fed liabilities for transactions instead of some other issuer," Jordan also said.
Jordan further predicted the public will determine the source -- private or federal -- of electronic money.

"Does the public want to use an electronic traveler's check issued by American Express, or an electronic Federal Reserve note?" Jordan asked. "The functional approach challenges bankers to determine how they can most efficiently perform the various financial functions their customers want."
But Jordan also said new technologies may alter the role played by traditional banks in the economy, as financial services on the Internet "will become the bank in people's mind, and in reality."
Such developments would also challenge the Fed's role as a bank regulator.
"As the financial marketplace evolves, so too must financial regulation and financial regulators," the Cleveland Fed president noted.
"Regulation should focus less on institutions and more on functions," Jordan said, while referring to a Bank Administration Institute's paper on performance-based regulation.
Jordan concluded technology is creating a need for cost-efficient changes in the regulatory process.
"The greatest disaster would not be a world without banks or bank regulators," he said. "Rather, it would be a drastic failure of innovation."
